talk: ROI (return on investment) is the profit an investment makes, as a share of what you put in. It lets you compare a small idea with a big one on the same scale. Always check whether the return is per year or in total.

terms.meaning: Gain divided by what you invested.
What you get back minus what you put in.
ROI per year, so projects of different lengths can be compared.

questions.prompt: You spend $20,000 on a fan zone for the season. It brings back $26,000. What's the ROI?
questions.hint: Gain divided by what you put in.
whyNot: That reads the $6,000 gain as 6%. ROI is the gain divided by the $20,000 invested.
$6,000 / $26,000 = about 23% divides by what came back. ROI divides by what you put in.
$26,000 / $20,000 = 130% counts your own money coming back too. The gain on top is 30%.

questions.prompt: Option A: put in $50,000, get $60,000 back in a year. Option B: put in $10,000, get $14,000 back in a year. Which has the better ROI?
questions.hint: Work out gain divided by cost for each.
working: B returns twice as much per dollar. A makes more dollars only because it's bigger.
whyNot: A's ROI is 20%, but B's is 40%. B is the better return per dollar.
A makes more dollars, but it also needs five times the money. Per dollar invested, B does twice as well.
Right pick, wrong reason. Cheap isn't the point. B wins because it returns 40% against A's 20%.

questions.prompt: A $200,000 gym upgrade makes a $60,000 gain in total, spread over 3 years. What's the ROI per year?
questions.hint: Total ROI first, then split it over the years.
working: Compare yearly ROI with yearly ROI, or a slow project will look better than it is.
whyNot: 30% is the ROI over all 3 years. Per year it's a third of that.
30% x 3 = 90% multiplies when you should divide. The 30% is already the total.
$60,000 / 3 = $20,000 is the gain per year in dollars. As a share of the $200,000 invested, it's 10%.

takeaway: ROI is gain divided by what you put in. Always ask: per year, or in total?
